title: Bitline-direct bonding: one bond per 16 bitlines
idea: MAGNIFY interface width down to the subarray: hybrid-bond each subarray's local I/O lines (one 1 um pad per 16 bitlines) straight to compute-die pads, deleting global I/O lines, column muxes, the DDR PHY and most of the DRAM periphery.
why: Periphery (~49% of die) and data-movement energy; claims ~30-40% more bits per DRAM wafer and <0.1 pJ/bit transfers.

title: Sense amplifiers reused as 50 mV link receivers
idea: MINIFY signal swing to ~50 mV by using the DRAM's own latch-type bitline sense-amplifier design (already built to resolve ~100 mV) as the receiver for low-swing differential links between DRAM and base die.
why: Voltage floor and pJ/bit: CV^2 energy on the link drops ~100x versus 0.4-0.5 V swing; claims ~0.05 pJ/bit inside the package.

title: Wafer-scale memory carpet replaces stacked HBM
idea: MAGNIFY the interposer to a full 300 mm passive silicon wafer and MINIFY stack height to one: ~200 single DRAM dies tile the wafer flat around ~20 accelerator dies, so every die is within ~5 mm of compute and needs no TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss): uses DDR-cost dies at HBM-class bandwidth; claims ~2-3x lower cost per GB/s.

title: Nano-TSVs through 5 um thinned DRAM dies
idea: MINIFY die thickness to ~5 um with backside-power-style wafer thinning so TSVs shrink to 0.5 um diameter, the size of ordinary vias, and the keep-out zone shrinks about 100x.
why: HBM TSV tax: TSV area overhead falls from ~5-10% to <0.5% and stress-related yield loss falls; claims ~15% more bits per stack wafer.

title: Diamond interlayers enabling 64-high cool stacks
idea: MAGNIFY stack height to 64 dies by bonding ~1 um polycrystalline-diamond heat-spreading films between DRAM layers in place of dummy thermal bumps, carrying heat sideways to the stack edge.
why: Density per package footprint and interposer area: 4x the capacity per HBM site without heat-induced refresh penalties.

title: DRAM bonded onto the backside of compute
idea: MINIFY vertical distance to ~10 um by hybrid-bonding DRAM to the back face of a backside-power-delivery logic wafer, with nano-vias interleaved with the power grid, so memory sits directly under every compute core.
why: Data-movement energy (HBM 3-4 pJ/bit): claims ~0.1 pJ/bit and removes the interposer entirely.

title: Sub-THz plastic waveguides for meter-scale memory links
idea: MAGNIFY carrier frequency to ~300 GHz and carry memory traffic over cheap polymer dielectric waveguides (~100 Gb/s per lane) from shared memory boxes up to 1-2 m away, with no lasers.
why: Interposer/CoWoS capacity and stranded memory: memory leaves the package at ~1-2 pJ/bit; pooling raises usable supply by ~20-30%.

title: XOR-delta writes: send only the changed bytes
idea: MINIFY write traffic: the base die keeps the old cache line, the host sends only the nonzero bytes of new XOR old plus a bitmask, and the base die patches the row with a masked write.
why: Data-movement energy and write bandwidth: optimizer, gradient and KV updates are often sparse in bytes; claims 2-4x less write traffic.

title: Laser-free DRAM via retro-modulated light from host
idea: MINIFY the photonics on the memory side to passive reflective microring modulators: the host's comb laser sends continuous-wave light to the DRAM base die, which modulates and reflects it back on the same fiber.
why: Data movement and thermals: no laser or SerDes PLL on the DRAM side; claims <1 pJ/bit off-package links and a cooler, cheaper memory module.

title: Charge-recycling stacked I/O drivers
idea: MINIFY I/O energy by stacking four driver domains in series between VDD and ground, so the charge spent toggling one lane's wire flows on to drive the next, with level-shifted receivers.
why: Interface energy per bit: ideal ~4x lower supply current for the I/O; claims ~2.5x in practice.

title: Million-wire DC memory with no SerDes or PLL
idea: MAGNIFY wire count to ~10^6/cm^2 with 1 um hybrid bonds and MINIFY each wire's rate to ~10 Mb/s: unterminated, unclocked CMOS levels with no SerDes, DLL or training, yet 10 Tb/s per cm^2.
why: Data-movement energy and PHY area: claims ~0.01-0.02 pJ/bit and deletes most of the DRAM I/O periphery.

title: Bit-plane memory layout for progressive-precision fetch
idea: MINIFY bits moved by storing tensors bit-plane by bit-plane (all MSBs together, then the next plane, and so on), so an accelerator fetches only the top N planes that the current layer or token needs.
why: Data-movement energy and effective capacity: 2-4x fewer bits moved for inference, with precision chosen per access.

title: Glass micro-bridges with copper and laser-written waveguides
idea: MINIFY the interposer to small ~1x2 mm glass bridges placed only where die edges meet, each carrying fine copper lines plus femtosecond-laser-inscribed optical waveguides for longer hops.
why: Interposer cost and capital (CoWoS capacity): ~95% less silicon interposer area, with optics on the same bridge.

title: Coarse pitch with 224G SerDes on organic substrate
idea: MAGNIFY bump pitch back to ~150-400 um and MAGNIFY lane speed to 224 Gb/s PAM4, attaching commodity LPDDR/DDR chiplets to accelerators on plain organic substrate with no silicon interposer.
why: Capital intensity and CoWoS bottleneck: memory bandwidth from abundant substrate capacity; claims ~5x cheaper packaging per GB at ~3-5 pJ/bit.

title: In-package mm-wave broadcast for weight multicast
idea: MAGNIFY fan-out: on-die 140 GHz antennas let one memory chiplet broadcast the same weights to 16 compute chiplets at once, instead of 16 point-to-point copies over the interposer.
why: Data movement for inference: weight traffic falls up to 16x when chiplets share layers; removes replicated weight copies.

title: YBCO superconducting interposer lines at 77 K
idea: MINIFY line loss to near zero: pattern YBCO superconducting traces on a sapphire interposer, cool the package with liquid nitrogen, and let memory sit centimeters away with lossless, low-swing transmission.
why: Data-movement energy: link energy limited only by drivers (~0.05 pJ/bit); cold DRAM also cuts leakage and refresh.

title: Few fast TSVs: 16 Gb/s per TSV
idea: MAGNIFY the rate per TSV to ~16 Gb/s with tiny on-die serializers, so ~90% of HBM data TSVs disappear (about 100 per stack instead of ~1,000+).
why: HBM TSV tax and yield: TSV area and defect count fall about 10x; claims +15-20% stack yield.

title: Reticle-stitched mega-DRAM wafer-bonded to logic
idea: MAGNIFY die size by stitching the DRAM array across 4+ reticles into one ~3,000 mm^2 die, bonded wafer-on-wafer to a logic wafer, with no dicing, no package I/O and no TSVs; row/column redundancy absorbs defects.
why: Packaging cost and data movement: removes the PHY and bumps; claims ~0.05 pJ/bit and terabytes per second per die.

title: Memory dust: fluidic self-assembled micro-DRAM chiplets
idea: MINIFY chiplets to ~0.5 mm^2 (128 Mb each) and place thousands of them into etched receptor sites on the compute wafer by shape-matched fluidic self-assembly, borrowing microLED mass-transfer methods.
why: Data movement and yield: memory is sprinkled within ~1 mm of every core, and known-good tiny dies yield >99%.

title: Clockless delay-insensitive memory interface
idea: MINIFY clocking to zero: replace the DDR clock, DLLs and training with 1-of-4 delay-insensitive handshake coding between DRAM and host, so the I/O idles at zero dynamic power.
why: Interface idle power (DLL/PLL is a large share of DRAM standby I/O): claims 30-50% lower interface power and no training time.

title: Full-row dump to a base-die SRAM row cache
idea: MAGNIFY transfer size to an entire 8 KB row: on activation, the row crosses an 8K-bit hybrid-bonded bus into a base-die SRAM row cache, the DRAM row closes at once, and random sub-reads are served from SRAM.
why: 128x overfetch and row hammer: the activated row is used fully and opened only once; claims ~3x less energy per useful bit.

title: Edge-standing die library: DRAM dies stood upright
idea: MAGNIFY dies per footprint by standing 100 thin DRAM dies upright like books, each bonded on one polished edge to the substrate through edge pads, with coolant flowing in the gaps between them.
why: Removes TSVs entirely and multiplies capacity per footprint about 10x versus a flat layout, with cooling built in.

title: Descriptor-driven memory with no command bus
idea: MINIFY command traffic: the host writes access descriptors (stride, gather list, tile shape) once, and the base die generates every address itself, so the bus carries only data.
why: Bus efficiency and data movement: claims 20-30% effective bandwidth gain, fewer pins, and fewer row misses through on-memory scheduling.

title: Inductive-coil stacks held by removable adhesive
idea: MINIFY the metallurgical bond to zero: dies talk through on-chip inductor coils, are stacked with a reworkable adhesive, and a failed die is peeled out and replaced with no bumps to reflow.
why: Removes TSVs and the HBM TSV tax; repairable stacks recover the 20-30% yield loss as rework instead of scrap.

title: Elastomer micro-socket for HBM on the interposer
idea: MINIFY socket pitch to ~100 um with an anisotropic conductive elastomer, so HBM stacks are clamped (not soldered) onto the interposer and can be swapped in the field.
why: HBM yield and lifetime: a bad stack no longer scraps a ~$30k accelerator; failed stacks go back for repair and reuse.

title: Free-space optical memory modules on kinematic mounts
idea: MINIFY contact to none: memory modules drop into a slot with a three-ball kinematic mount, and lenses align free-space optical beams to the host, so there are no connectors to wear and modules swap tool-free.
why: Off-package memory at ~1-2 pJ/bit with field-replaceable, reusable modules; frees interposer area.

title: Harvest-and-rebin HBM from retired accelerators
idea: MAGNIFY HBM's useful life: base dies carry standard re-ball pads and a full built-in self-test, so stacks pulled from retired GPUs are retested, graded and rebonded into CXL memory expanders.
why: Scarce-resource and capital intensity: second-life memory adds supply without wafers; claims 10-20% extra effective bits per year.

title: Gallium liquid-metal microbumps in micro-wells
idea: MINIFY the melting point to ~30 C: microbumps are galinstan-filled wells capped by a dielectric frame, so a die lifts off with gentle heat and reseats with the wells reformed.
why: Rework and recycling of stacked memory; dies come out clean with no solder residue, cutting scrap and tin use.

title: Capacitive proximity tiles aligned by micro-magnets
idea: MINIFY the gap to a ~1 um dielectric: memory tiles clamp face-to-face with compute and signal through capacitive coupling pads at 10 um pitch, aligned by patterned micro-magnets; unclamp to replace.
why: No TSVs, bumps or solder; ~0.1 pJ/bit links, with full disassembly for repair or recovery.

title: Water-soluble release layer under the interposer
idea: MINIFY end-of-life separation cost: a polymer release layer between interposer and dies dissolves in hot water, so dies, interposer and substrate separate cleanly for reuse or pure-stream recycling.
why: Recyclability and scarce materials: recovers whole known-good dies and high-purity Cu and Si instead of shredded mixed waste.

title: Hot-spare die plus empty bond site per stack
idea: MAGNIFY redundancy to the whole die: each HBM stack ships with one spare DRAM die and base-die bypass switches that logically replace a failing die in the field, plus an open top site for a later add-on die.
why: Field repair and HBM yield: a dead die no longer kills the stack; claims +10-15% shipped yield and longer life.

title: Pluggable memory modules in an optical transceiver form factor
idea: MINIFY the replacement unit to a faceplate-pluggable module in an OSFP-like case holding DRAM plus a photonic link, hot-swapped like a network transceiver.
why: Memory pooled and serviceable at the rack edge; GPU packages no longer lock in memory; better utilization and repair.

title: Mono-material all-silicon memory package
idea: MINIFY material diversity to one: a silicon interposer, silicon lid and silicon stiffener joined by oxide-oxide and Cu-Cu bonds, with no epoxy mold, gold or solder, so the whole package is one recycling stream.
why: Recyclability and scarce resources: avoids gold, tin and tungsten chokepoints and makes silicon/copper recovery simple.

title: Swappable PHY adapter chiplet keeps DRAM across generations
idea: MAGNIFY memory lifetime to three compute generations: the DRAM stack talks a fixed simple die-to-die protocol, and only a small reworkable adapter chiplet is swapped to match each new host PHY.
why: Capital and supply: memory is reused across 6-9 years instead of 3, about doubling bits served per wafer made.

title: Copper nanowire velcro: re-mateable room-temperature interconnects
idea: MINIFY bonding heat to zero: dense interdigitated Cu nanowire arrays on both faces interlock at room temperature like nano-velcro, giving electrical contact that can be pulled apart and re-mated several times.
why: Removes solder and tin and allows rework of memory chiplets; claims ~20 um pitch with 5+ re-mating cycles.

title: On-die health passport for second-life grading
idea: MAGNIFY what each die knows about its own history: an on-die tamper-proof log of power-on hours, ECC events, row-hammer counts and temperature lets refurbishers grade stacks instantly.
why: Second-life supply: cheap trustworthy grading makes reused DRAM sellable, adding usable bits without new fabs.

title: Diels-Alder reversible underfill that unzips at 120 C
idea: MINIFY rework damage: the underfill is a thermally reversible Diels-Alder polymer network that depolymerizes near 120 C, so microbumped memory dies lift off cleanly and re-underfill afterward.
why: Repairable 2.5D/3D packages; a bad HBM or chiplet is reworked instead of scrapping the whole module.

title: Self-healing links with spare lanes and field remap
idea: MAGNIFY lane redundancy to ~10% spares with a base-die crossbar that keeps checking bump and TSV margins in service and retires links degraded by electromigration on the fly.
why: Lifetime and yield: packages repair their own wires instead of failing; claims 2x interconnect lifetime.

title: Persistent glass memory backplane with consumable compute
idea: MAGNIFY substrate life: DRAM is embedded in cavities of a long-lived glass-core backplane, and compute chiplets land on top through reversible bumps and are swapped every generation.
why: Capital intensity: memory, the expensive scarce part, is installed once and serves many compute upgrades.

title: Laser-coded material tags plus memory take-back policy
idea: MINIFY sorting cost: every memory package carries a laser-etched material bill of Cu/Sn/Si/Au, read by automated shredder lines, under an extended-producer-responsibility rule for DRAM.
why: U.S. scarce-resource recovery: makes recycled Cu, Sn and Au streams economic and gives domestic secondary supply.

title: Sacrificial backside allows one debond and re-thin cycle
idea: MAGNIFY reuse cycles: HBM dies keep a ~10 um sacrificial backside margin, so a debonded die can be re-thinned, re-polished and hybrid-bonded once more into a new stack.
why: Recovers known-good DRAM dies from failed or retired stacks, cutting wafer demand per shipped GB.

title: Infrared optical vertical links through bondless stacks
idea: MINIFY metal in the vertical path to zero: 1.3 um infrared emitters and photodiodes send light straight through the silicon dies (silicon is transparent there), so stacked dies need no TSVs and can be separated.
why: Removes the TSV tax and makes stacks separable for repair or recycling; claims ~0.5 pJ/bit vertical links.

title: Open replaceable memory chiplet standard tied to procurement
idea: MAGNIFY interchangeability: an open mechanical and electrical spec for socketed memory chiplets (UCIe-style), required in federally funded AI clusters, so any vendor's memory can be swapped.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply resilience: new domestic memory makers can sell into installed systems; repair beats scrap.

title: Memory leasing with guaranteed take-back and refurbishment
idea: MINIFY ownership: vendors lease HBM and CXL modules, take them back at end of term, refurbish and redeploy them, which gives them a financial reason to design for disassembly.
why: Effective supply and capital: each module serves 2-3 lifecycles; cuts buyer capex at a time when prices have risen 4x.

title: Four-high replaceable memory bricks in a 2D array
idea: MINIFY the repair unit: instead of 12- to 16-high stacks, use many 4-high bricks tiled flat on the substrate, each individually removable, so a failure costs one small brick.
why: HBM yield (stack yield compounds per die) and repair cost: claims ~2x better stack yield and cheap field swaps.

title: Shape-memory alloy clamps that release chiplets at 80 C
idea: MINIFY disassembly effort: NiTi clamps hold memory chiplets on pressure contacts and spring open when the package is heated to ~80 C in a recycling oven, so dies drop out intact.
why: Recyclability with zero labor: separates dies, substrate and lid automatically for reuse or pure material streams.
